seo.title: Karmic tail 12 7 22 compatibility: Hanged Man, Chariot, Fool
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 7 22 compatibility: why a couple lives in “not now” for years, who holds the reins, and how The Fool asks them to use the door, not the window.

title: Karmic tail 12-7-22 in compatibility: the long “not now” and the leap from the window
short: The couple's tail 12-7-22 sets a strange riddle: how do two people who can wait for years suddenly decide in a second — and jump the wrong way? The answer is written in three cards, and they have to be read in order. The entry to the task is The Hanged Man: the couple's common language sounds like “not now”, and both are happy to hand their step to a third person. The middle of the task is The Chariot: movement arrives, often someone else's, and everything depends on who holds the reins. The main task is The Fool: learning a freedom that walks out through the door instead of jumping out of the window.

sections.h2: Gogol's Marriage: a tail played out in two acts
paragraphs: In 1842 Gogol published a comedy subtitled “an utterly incredible event in two acts”. He had started it in 1833 as Zhenikhi (The Suitors) and finished it abroad in 1841, so the play itself hung in suspense for eight years. The plot fits in one line: a bridegroom escapes from his own wedding through a window. But read Zhenitba (Marriage) with the cards 12-7-22 in hand and three acts show through, in the order of the tail. Quotations from the play follow E. L. Voynich's translation of 1895; where her version is abridged, the translation is ours and marked as such.

The play opens on a man lying down. Podkolyosin, a court counsellor, smokes his pipe on the sofa. The matchmaker has been calling “for the last three months”, the tailcoat is being made, the boot polish has been bought, and he sighs: “here one goes on, living and living; and one ends by getting quite disgusted with everything. There, I've let the time slip by once more.” He cannot go and see the bride: the weather is dull, “if I go out, I may get caught in the rain.” When the matchmaker describes him to the bride she does not even give his name, but her portrait is exact: “such a slow stick-in-the-mud, there's no getting him out of the house.”

Then his friend Kochkaryov bursts in and goes straight for the same matchmaker: “What the devil did you marry me for?” A minute later he is marrying off somebody else: “Now, my lad, this business mustn't be put off — put on your hat and come along.” In a single day Kochkaryov sees off the rivals, persuades the bride that the other suitors are brawlers, orders the supper, sends for the carriage and dispatches the guests straight to church.

The finale is a leap. The groom is alone in the room, the carriage is at the porch, there are people at the door. He climbs onto the window sill, says “Lord, give Thy blessing!” and drops into the street, and from offstage comes: “Oh! oh! It's a good height though! Hi, drozhki!” The last line goes to the matchmaker: “If he'd run out by the door it would have been another thing, but when the bridegroom pops out of window all I can say is — I wish you joy!”

The play is usually retold as a joke about an indecisive man. But 12-7-22 is the tail of a couple, not of a person, and Gogol, looked at closely, wrote a play about a couple too. The bride speaks the same language.

sections.h2: Entry to the task, 12 — The Hanged Man: the common language of “not now”
paragraphs: For Lisovskaya the entry to the task is what the couple wants together: shared wishes, agreements, a “common language”. The point sits on the line of tasks, so the same wish can also work as resistance. In the tail 12-7-22 this place belongs to The Hanged Man, the card of life held in suspension. What such a couple wants together is not to get it wrong: to wait for the right moment, to be sure, not to fall. Their common language is postponement.

In Marriage both of them speak it. Podkolyosin, already in his tailcoat, tells his friend: “I think you'd better go alone.” Agafya Tikhonovna, with the suitors in the room, whispers to her aunt: “Auntie! stop here instead of me!” He sums up his bachelor life: “I have lived and lived, served, gone to the Department, dined, slept.” She weeps on her wedding day: “I lived and lived — and now I have to get married!” (our translation). For three months he keeps asking his servant whether the tailcoat is coming along and whether the polish shines. She cannot choose a suitor, draws lots — and pulls every slip out of her reticule at once: “Oh! oh! they've all come out!”

And the decisive minute is one they share. Already in her wedding dress, the bride comes into the room and thinks: “Oh! I wish he weren't in the room just this minute; I wish he'd gone out!” The wish comes true to the letter: he is no longer there. **One of them ran, but both of them wanted it** — that is the common language of this tail.

Lisovskaya describes couples with The Hanged Man as if she had read Gogol: they take a long time to enter a relationship, and to marry they need a push from outside — she puts it more bluntly, a kick. In the plus these are delicate, tactful people: they always listen, they sense each other at a distance, and often one does nothing for themselves and everything for the other. Gogol's couple has its plus as well. After their only conversation alone, about the weather, flowers and an outing, both are pleased. “What a superior person! … The best of all is that he doesn't talk small talk,” she says. “I passed the time most agreeably,” he says. At their own slow pace, these two suit each other.

The minus of The Hanged Man in a couple is a life lived for other people's eyes: what others will think and say matters more than what happens inside. For Podkolyosin this is exactly what blocks the door. Before he jumps, he reasons: “there are heaps of people at the door, and everywhere, and they'd ask me why.” In Waite's list of divinatory meanings the reversed Hanged Man includes “the crowd”. The crowd stands in the doorway, and only one exit is left.

Today the language sounds different, but it is instantly recognisable. Two people have lived together for seven years and have discussed the wedding five times: “after the renovation”, “once things settle down with Mum”, “let's do it in summer”. Nobody is against it — each is sure they are waiting for the other. In the end the question is asked not by either of them but by a sister at a family dinner: “So when is it happening?”

sections.h2: Middle of the task, 7 — The Chariot: someone else's carriage and your own cab
paragraphs: The middle of a couple's tail has no meaning of its own in the book: Lisovskaya calls it an addition to the main task. We read it as the road — what the couple does and goes through on the way from the wish at the entry to the task at the end. Here the road is The Chariot: movement, will, the journey. In Russian the word for chariot, kolesnitsa, is built on koleso, “wheel”, and the hero who is supposed to climb into it is called Podkolyosin — a name in which you hear pod kolesom, “under the wheel”. Beside him stands Kochkaryov, whose name echoes kochka, a bump in the road. The literary scholar V. Prozorov pointed out the meaning that arises when these two surnames are read together.

This couple's Chariot often comes from outside. Benebell Wen writes that the charioteer's will can be received: strong external forces “have put the momentum in the Seeker”, which is why the card, for all its outward activity, is “intrinsically yin” — receptive by nature. For The Hanged Man, who needs a push, this is good news: momentum can come from a friend, from family, from circumstances. The only question is whether borrowed momentum becomes a direction of one's own.

Kochkaryov is The Chariot in its purest form. Waite calls the charioteer “above all things triumph in the mind” and adds that “the planes of his conquest are manifest or external and not within himself”. Kochkaryov conquers everything external: the bride's consent, the aunt, the rivals, the supper, the carriage, the guests. Inside the groom he moves nothing at all. Left alone, he cannot tell where he is driving: “And what am I to him — nurse, maiden aunt, mother-in-law, sponsor? … Sometimes there's no making out what a man does a thing for!” Gogol's stage direction for this monologue says that he walks up and down “in strong motion” (in Voynich, “in great agitation”). A Chariot without a goal of its own drives in circles.

Lisovskaya describes two minuses of The Chariot in a couple: a passive one — aimlessness, routine, draining each other's motivation — and an active one: haste, conclusions and events rushed, one partner bending to fit the other. In Marriage they take turns within a single day: three months on the sofa, then “it will be time to go to church and be married in an hour.” Podkolyosin, by the way, asks for something reasonable: “I must have at least a month breathing-time.” In reply Kochkaryov falls on his knees, curses him, wishes that “a tipsy cabman would drive his shafts down your throat”, and later catches him up and shoves him back into the room with both hands. **Here the mechanism of the tail is visible like a blueprint: a “not now” that nobody hears goes out of the window.**

There are two vehicles in the play. Kochkaryov has ordered the carriage for the wedding, and it waits at the porch. Joining the hands of bride and groom, he delivers a little sermon: “Marriage is a kind of thing… It's not like hailing a cab and driving off somewhere; it's a duty of quite another kind” (our translation). A few minutes later the groom does exactly what marriage was compared with: he calls a cab himself — “Hi, drozhki! … All right! Make haste!” — and Dunyashka, the girl of the house, reports it in the same words: “he took a drozhki and drove away.” It is the only time in the whole play that Podkolyosin gives orders to a driver. He does become his own charioteer — but he drives the other way. As for what kind of “duty” marriage is, Kochkaryov promised to explain “afterwards” and never got the chance.

A strong Chariot looks different: the two are quick to get moving, they decide together and fast, each has a road of their own, but they travel in the same direction. Lisovskaya advises such couples not to hurry each other and to settle, clearly and without hints, the status of the relationship and each one's role. A good scene: one of them is offered a job in another city, and the question “shall we go together?” comes up over dinner before the contract is signed, not after. A worrying scene: a move they planned together happens when one of them has already paid the deposit, and the other first hears of it as a done deal.

sections.h2: Main task, 22 — The Fool: a freedom that leaves by the door
paragraphs: Lisovskaya reads a couple's main task mostly through the minus. Her key to The Fool is freedom: in the plus it is the trust that gives freedom, in the minus it is freedom without boundaries and without responsibility. Her description of The Fool in a couple reads like a summary of Gogol's plot: the relationship starts easily and cheerfully, problems arrive as soon as it comes to serious steps, people run away from difficulties and then blame the partner for it. The main thing stays unclear — what these two are to each other.
In Marriage this formula is spoken by the sailor Zhevakin, turned down for the seventeenth time: “At first everything goes all right; and then, when the critical moment comes, they always refuse me.”

In Waite's list of divinatory meanings the reversed Fool includes “absence”. Gogol gives it an exact formula. The bride searches the house for the groom: “— We can't find Ivan Kuzmich. — Can't find him? Has he gone out? — No, he hasn't gone out either.” **“Not here and not gone out” — this is what the minus of The Fool looks like in a couple**: the person is close by, and yet not there; nothing has been said, nothing decided. Lisovskaya describes the same minus from the outside: a couple in name, living like neighbours and doing everything apart.

Kochkaryov, peering under the chairs, adds that the groom “couldn't vanish without going out of the room”. In Russian the verb for “to vanish”, propast', is also the noun propast', a precipice — the very edge on which The Fool stands. Podkolyosin did both: he vanished, and he jumped.

The Fool appears in the play before the window, in the only conversation between bride and groom. Podkolyosin tells her that on the road he takes to the Department every day he passed a plasterer: working men “will stand right on the top”, and this one was “afraid of nothing”. “What a daring race the Russians are!” he marvels. A line earlier he counts on his fingers the days until the outing to Ekaterinhof and arrives at: “in twenty-two days.” Gogol knew nothing of the destiny matrix, so this is a coincidence. But a conversation that began with “Do you like going for rides, madam?” (our translation) has arrived at twenty-two and at a man who stands on a height without fear. The groom admires him from below, from the pavement.

The tail's main task is not “marry at any cost”. The matchmaker's last line matters more than it seems: had the groom run out by the door, “it would have been another thing”. The Fool's freedom includes the right to say “no” and the right to say “not now” — but aloud, face to face, through the door. The window is the same freedom with the words taken away: someone leaves without a word of explanation, and the other is left with the question “not here and not gone out?” Lisovskaya gives couples with The Fool two pieces of advice that seem to pull in opposite directions: give the partner freedom without checks — and think about responsibility before serious steps. **The door is freedom that answers for itself in words.**

Wen describes The Fool as a fork in the road: the next step can send the Seeker “flying into the air over that cliff with impressive accomplishment” — or down, “from naïveté”. She ties The Hanged Man to the same question: will the Seeker fall or fly? The tail 12-7-22 begins and ends with this question: first it is put to the couple, then it becomes their task.

A scene from life: the wedding date is set, the venue is paid for, and a week before, one of the two suddenly has a work emergency — a business trip, a crunch, “let's move it”. The other agrees and feels a relief they do not admit even to themselves. They opened the window together.

sections.h2: Waite: two figures above the void
paragraphs: Lay Waite's cards side by side and you see that the tail begins and ends with a halt. The Hanged Man hangs head downwards by one ankle, his arms bound behind him, and his face, in Waite's words, expresses “deep entrancement, not suffering”. The Fool stands still too: a young man “pauses at the brink of a precipice among the great heights of the world”, and Waite specifies that the urge to walk is still visible in him, “though he is stationary at the given moment”. Both are above the void. The difference is what holds each one there: The Hanged Man is held by a rope, The Fool holds himself.

The Hanged Man's bound arms are in the play as well. The groom never asks for the bride's hand; Kochkaryov does it for him — “he asks your hand”. Afterwards Podkolyosin takes her hand and exclaims “What a lovely little hand!” — but the proposal has already been spoken in someone else's voice.

To whoever understands The Hanged Man, Waite promises “intimations concerning a great awakening that is possible”. Podkolyosin's awakening comes five minutes before the window: “Now, at last, only now, I know what life is; a new world has opened before me.” For a couple with this tail the awakening can be real. The passage from awakening to step is no longer The Hanged Man but The Chariot, and that is exactly where the story breaks.

Of The Fool at the edge Waite writes: “The edge which opens on the depth has no terror; it is as if angels were waiting to uphold him, if it came about that he leaped from the height.” Podkolyosin also asks for support from above — “Lord, give Thy blessing!” — and jumps. The gesture is the same; the direction is not. Waite's Fool looks at the expanse of sky rather than the prospect below, and steps forward; Podkolyosin jumps away from the door. **The Fool steps because he trusts. Podkolyosin jumps because he is afraid.** The couple's main task is to turn the second leap into the first.

sections.h2: The numbers: who brings these cards into the couple
paragraphs: Every point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, reduced to 22. Running through every date shows that the tail 12-7-22 is built from only four combinations of personal tails: 18-3-12 + 21-4-10 (65% of such couples), 6-17-11 + 6-17-11 (18%), 3-22-19 + 9-12-3 (17%) and the very rare 6-14-8 + 6-20-14, a fraction of a per cent. These combinations show who brings what.

Neither partner ever has The Chariot in their personal tail — not in a single such couple. Nobody owns the vehicle: it is assembled only from the sum. In two couples out of three it is made of one partner's Empress and the other's Emperor (3 + 4) — the home and the order. When Kochkaryov talks his friend round, he paints exactly these two cards: “Here there'll be a sofa, there a lap-dog, then a birdcage, and fancy-work lying about”, children, “a whole half-dozen” — and the order that the bachelor admits he lacks. In one couple in six the middle is plainer still: 22 + 12 = 34 → 7, so The Chariot is made of one partner's Fool and the other's Hanged Man. **The couple's vehicle is literally assembled from the other two cards of its tail.**

The Hanged Man, by contrast, is nearly always already familiar to one of the two. In 82% of such couples he is in one partner's personal tail: in 65% as that partner's personal main task, in 17% as the middle. The postponement that becomes a shared language often belonged to one person first.

The couple's Fool is always an exact sum of the two personal main tasks, with no reduction: 12 + 10, 11 + 11, 19 + 3, 8 + 14. In the most common case it is one partner's Hanged Man plus the other's Wheel of Fortune: a suspended man and a turning wheel add up to a leap. You can hear this arithmetic in Podkolyosin's name, too. The Fool appears in a personal tail in only 17% of such couples, and then in one partner only.

In 18% of couples none of the three cards appears in either personal tail. Almost all of them are couples with identical personal tails, 6-17-11: two entries of The Lovers give The Hanged Man (6 + 6), two Stars in the middle give The Chariot (17 + 17 = 34 → 7), two Strengths in the main task give The Fool (11 + 11). Two similar people, and a tail that neither of them has.

This tail has no permutations: the same numbers in another order never occur in a couple's chart. There is, however, a tail with the same ends and a different middle — 12-16-22, where The Tower stands between “not now” and freedom. There, freedom is reached through a collapse. In 12-7-22 it is reached by road.

sections.h2: Atmosphere and values: a Star that no person has
paragraphs: In 81.9% of couples with this tail the centre of the chart — the atmosphere inside the couple — is The Star, 17. No person ever has The Star at the centre of a personal chart: this card in the centre exists only for two. And with it the couple's tail obeys the laws of a personal tail: the entry equals the main task plus the centre (22 + 17 = 39 → 12), the middle equals the entry plus the task (12 + 22 = 34 → 7). In arithmetic terms such a couple is a single person with The Star at the centre — someone who is never born. That person appears only when these two are together.

For Lisovskaya, The Star in the atmosphere is a union that inspires both; often only next to each other do people understand who they want to be. This is Gogol's “a new world has opened before me”. The Star's minus is the same story from the other end: people enjoy being in love but take no responsibility, and may part as soon as marriage or a child comes up. In his dreams Podkolyosin gets to taste “such bliss as one only hears about in fairy-tales” — and jumps. The Star gives the couple a dream; The Fool demands a step.

In the remaining 18.1% the centre is Justice, 8. Such couples, according to Lisovskaya, take a long time to look at each other and a long time to settle in. In the plus they want to make the relationship official and fair; in the minus they do not want to make it official and they break promises. It is the same question of pace, only settled by weighing rather than by dreaming.

The couple's values — the point that says what the union exists for — are held by The Lovers in 71.5% of such couples and by The Devil in 28.5%. These are two sides of Gogol's fear. The Lovers is the card of choice, and choice is exactly what torments Agafya Tikhonovna: “Really, it is a very difficult thing to have to choose.” The Devil is the card of bonds, and bonds are exactly what frighten Podkolyosin: “For all one's life, for ever — you can't get over the fact that you're tying yourself.” Lisovskaya's conclusion about The Devil is that nobody belongs to anybody. For seven couples in ten, the value of the union is to choose each other consciously, and more than once; for three in ten, it is to build a bond that holds without shackling.
How the tail adds up in practice can be seen on two dates that the site's engine gives for it.

The partner born on 05.12.1975 has the personal tail 18-3-12 — The Moon, The Empress, The Hanged Man — and a centre of 6. The partner born on 14.10.1975 has 21-4-10: The World, The Emperor, The Wheel of Fortune, and a centre of 11. The couple's entry: 18 + 21 = 39, and 3 + 9 = 12. The middle: 3 + 4 = 7. The main task: 12 + 10 = 22, with no reduction. The couple's centre is 6 + 11 = 17, The Star; the values are 15, The Devil.

In this couple The Fool also stands on the point “What to create together” (the birth months: 12 + 10 = 22), and The Hanged Man on “Where it sparks” (7 + 5 = 12). This happens in 3% and 4% of couples with this tail. Lisovskaya reads “What to create together” only in the plus: for these two, freedom is not only a task but also something to build together. And The Hanged Man in the place of quarrels hints at where they come from: from a wait that has dragged on and never been named.

sections.h2: How to get out of the tail: the door instead of the window
paragraphs: A couple's tail is neither a verdict nor a forecast: it is a script that can be recognised and rewritten. Gogol's play shows the worst version of it, and the same play shows where it breaks.

ul: **Name your windows.** Each of the two has a habitual exit for the moment a step becomes serious: work, a trip, the parents, “I need to think”, silence. If the windows are named on a calm day, it is harder to slip out through them unnoticed on a difficult one.

**Say “not now” through the door.** With a reason and a date: “I'm not ready — let's come back to this in March.” Podkolyosin asked for a month, and the request was reasonable. The mistake was that nobody heard it and he did not stand up for it.

**Choose your own pace.** A push from outside — from friends, family, circumstances — does The Hanged Man good. But the route is chosen by the couple, by the two of them, and they get into one carriage, not two different ones.
**Freedom plus a word.** Don't check up on each other and don't hold each other back — and don't vanish in silence. Freedom that answers for itself in words is the strong version of The Fool.

paragraphs: The strong version of this couple looks like this. The Hanged Man gives it depth: these two know how to listen, they don't rush feelings, and they see each other from unexpected angles. The Chariot gives shared movement: moves, common roads, and a road of one's own for each. The Fool gives trust and lightness: such couples start again easily and are not afraid of the unknown. The conversation that Podkolyosin never had takes place in their kitchen: “I'm not ready yet. Let's say March — and in March I'll give an honest answer, yes or no.” And in March that conversation really happens.

intro: The tail 12-7-22 turns up in about one couple in 91, which puts it 33rd among the 97 couple tails. People also search for it as a “12-7-22 programme in the destiny matrix”, but no single person has such a programme. In a personal chart the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and with The Fool as the main task an entry of 12 would need a centre of 17 — and no person ever has The Star at the centre. These three numbers only come together for two people. Lisovskaya calls the couple's tail its karmic programme and reads it above all through the minus: through what the couple cannot manage and has to learn.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 12-7-22 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of a couple's chart: The Hanged Man at the entry to the task, The Chariot in the middle, The Fool as the main task. The story runs from a shared “not now”, through movement that often arrives from outside, to a task of freedom: learning to take a serious step openly, “through the door”, rather than vanishing.

faq.q: Is there a 12-7-22 programme in a personal destiny matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal chart the entry of the tail equals the main task plus the centre, and with The Fool as the main task an entry of 12 would need a centre of 17, while no person has The Star at the centre. The triple 12-7-22 only arises as a couple's tail; Lisovskaya calls a couple's tail its karmic programme.

faq.q: Does this tail mean the couple will never reach the wedding?
faq.a: No. The tail describes a task, not an outcome, and predicts nothing. It shows where the couple is thin-skinned: in long postponement, in someone else's pace and in the temptation to vanish instead of talking. Couples with this tail live both married and unmarried; their task is the same — to take their steps openly.

faq.q: Who plays Podkolyosin in the couple?
faq.a: Either of the two, and more often both in turn: the roles do not depend on gender. In the play both the groom and the bride want to put off the step, and in life the part of Kochkaryov may be played by a partner, by family or by circumstances.

faq.q: How do you work out a couple's tail from the dates of birth?
faq.a: Every point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, reduced to 22. The entry to the task is the sum of the two personal tail entries, the middle is the sum of the personal middles, the main task is the sum of the personal karmic tasks. The couple's middle is not recalculated from its ends: it is added up from the two personal middles.

report: The most decisive act in Gogol's Marriage is performed by its most indecisive man. For three months the matchmaker has been calling on Podkolyosin, a court counsellor, and still he cannot go and see the bride: the weather is dull, “if I go out, I may get caught in the rain.” Yet he jumps out of a window and away from his own wedding in a single minute. The couple's karmic tail 12-7-22 tells the same story in the same order: The Hanged Man, The Chariot, The Fool. Two people can wait for years, then decide in a second — and jump the wrong way.

report.h3: One of them ran, but both of them wanted it

report: The entry to the task is the couple's common language, what the two want together. Here stands The Hanged Man, the card of life held in suspension, and the common language sounds like “not now”. The play is usually read as a joke about a timid groom, but the bride speaks the same language. Podkolyosin, already in his tailcoat, tells his friend he had “better go alone”. Agafya Tikhonovna, with the suitors in the room, whispers to her aunt: “Auntie! stop here instead of me!” He: “I have lived and lived, served, gone to the Department.” She: “I lived and lived — and now I have to get married!” And at the decisive minute the bride, in her wedding dress, thinks: “Oh! I wish he weren't in the room just this minute; I wish he'd gone out!” The wish comes true to the letter. **One of them ran, but both of them wanted it.**

In Lisovskaya's reading such couples take a long time to enter a relationship, and to marry they need a push from outside. In the plus these are tactful people who know how to listen and sense each other at a distance. After their only conversation alone, Gogol's bride and groom are pleased with each other: at their own slow pace, they suit. The minus of The Hanged Man is a life lived for other people's eyes. Before he jumps, Podkolyosin reasons: “there are heaps of people at the door, and everywhere, and they'd ask me why.” In Waite's list of divinatory meanings the reversed Hanged Man includes “the crowd”. The crowd stands in the doorway, and only one exit is left.

report.h3: Someone else's carriage and a cab of one's own

report: The middle of the task is The Chariot: movement that arrives, often from outside. In the play it is brought by his friend Kochkaryov: “Now, my lad, this business mustn't be put off… come along.” In one day he sees off the rivals, orders the supper, sends for the carriage and dispatches the guests to church. Waite writes that the charioteer's conquests are “manifest or external and not within himself”. Kochkaryov conquers everything except the groom himself.

Neither partner has The Chariot in their personal tail: the two own no vehicle of their own, it is assembled only from their sum. That is why it is so easy to climb into someone else's. Podkolyosin asks for something reasonable — “I must have at least a month breathing-time” — and is told the wedding is in an hour. **A “not now” that nobody hears goes out of the window.** Joining the hands of bride and groom, Kochkaryov lectures them: “It's not like hailing a cab and driving off somewhere; it's a duty of quite another kind.” A few minutes later the groom does exactly what marriage was compared with: he calls a cab himself — “All right! Make haste!” He does become his own charioteer — but he drives the other way.

report.h3: Not here and not gone out

report: The main task is The Fool, and Lisovskaya's key to the card is freedom. In the minus, couples with The Fool start easily, and problems arrive as soon as it comes to serious steps; the main thing stays unclear — what these two are to each other. In Waite's list of divinatory meanings the reversed Fool includes “absence”, and Gogol gives it an exact formula. The gesture is the same; the direction is not. **The Fool steps because he trusts; Podkolyosin jumps because he is afraid.** The couple's main task is to turn the second leap into the first.

report.h3: Had he run out by the door, it would have been another thing

report: Gogol gives the play's last line to the matchmaker: “If he'd run out by the door it would have been another thing, but when the bridegroom pops out of window…” That line holds the way out. The tail's task is not “marry at any cost”. The Fool's freedom includes the right to say “no” and the right to say “not now” — but aloud, face to face, through the door. Lisovskaya advises such couples to give the partner freedom without checks — and to think about responsibility before serious steps. **The door is freedom that answers for itself in words.**

In practice this means naming the windows on a calm day: work, a trip, the parents, “I need to think”, silence. Saying “not now” with a reason and a date. Accepting a push from outside, but choosing the route together and getting into one carriage. The strong version of a couple with this tail is the depth of The Hanged Man, the shared road of The Chariot and the trust of The Fool. The conversation that Podkolyosin never had takes place in such a couple's kitchen: “I'm not ready yet. Let's say March — and in March I'll give an honest answer, yes or no.” And in March that conversation really happens.

unit.title: The door, not the window

captions.M: Waiting for the right moment and putting off the step
captions.N: Choosing your own pace, not someone else's carriage
captions.D: Not vanishing in silence, but saying yes or no at the door

unit.meaning: Your task is to take serious steps openly: say “no” or “not now” out loud instead of slipping away, as if through a window.
